newsitem.title: ZAIRE: UN seeks return home of refugees trapped in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: UN seeks return home of refugees trapped in Zaire.

text.p: U.N. refugee supremo Sadako Ogata is seeking ways of repatriating Zaire's remaining Rwandan Hutu refugees who are trapped by civil war in the east of the sprawling and chaotic Central African nation.

Ogata told reporters in the capital Kinshasa on Friday that she was looking at options with the government, whose forces are battling Tutsi-led rebels for control of a string of towns on several fronts.

In New York, the U.N. Security Council called for an end to hostilities, the withdrawal of all foreign forces from Zaire, including mercenaries fighting alongside the army, and demanded that combatants respect the rights of refugees.
"It underlines the obligations of all concerned to respect the relevant provisions of international humanitarian law," the council said in a statement after a formal meeting on the war.

Ogata, on the first leg of a trip to Central Africa's troubled Great Lakes region, met the government on the plight of the estimated 300,000 refugees who fled west in December when many more fellow Hutus opted to return home.
"In theory, there are two ways of repatriating the refugees, by plane or by road through safety corridors," she said.

Ogata was due on Saturday to visit Tingi Tingi where 120,000 weak and frightened refugees gathered after fleeing with Hutu hardliners blamed for Rwanda's 1994 genocide but security concerns put a question mark over the trip.

Relief agencies pulled their international staff out of Tingi Tingi and the nearby town of Lubutu on Friday after panicky Zairean soldiers fired in the air and demanded money and vehicles from aid agencies.
Lubutu is 200 km (125 miles) from Kisangani, headquarters of a counter-offensive that Zaire's army launched on January 20.
Aid workers reported refugees fleeing towards Lubutu from Amisi, further down the road to the rebel-held east.
A senior defence official in Kinshasa reported heavy fighting around the gold and tin mining town of Punia south of Lubutu.
"The rebels are more numberous than us at Punia and there is a great risk they will take the town," he said.
The rebels responded to the much-trumpeted government counter-offensive by attacking on several fronts.
Both sides have reported the fall or recapture of a handful of towns in the war zone, which stretches from a corner of the mineral-rich southern province of Shaba to the north east.
Rebels say they hold a large strip of territory along the borders with Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda.
Zaire, which accuses Rwanda and Uganda of invading in support of the rebels, said on Friday its army had retaken Watsa in the north east and Shabunda in the east.
Zairean officials spoke of killing 800 rebels and taking Ugandan soldiers prisoners at Watsa.
In the past, they have displayed Ugandan and Rwandan prisoners in Kinshasa.
Veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko, meanwhile, returned to his Gbadolite jungle palace on Friday after medical tests in Europe.
Mobutu, who had prostate surgery in August, denied asking Morocco for military help on a visit on his way home.
